meta.title: Selekoa historical research sample
meta.scope: Selected historical records, 1965–2024, plus prior roles with unknown dates. Genesis source checks are dated 2026-09-17; personnel-continuity checks are dated 2026-09-18. Human source review pending. Not a current or comprehensive sector inventory. Governance version histories through July 2026, researched September 18, 2026; policy text is not evidence of implementation. Selected capital and compute records through April 2026; transaction stages do not imply current arrangements or realised spending. Targeted corrections dated 2026-09-25: one attributed claim accepted after explicit human source review; a second narrowly scoped résumé passage is human-reviewed. Other seed claims remain pending. Intellectual Lineage II adds selected oversight citations and agenda reception, checked 2026-09-25; all new records remain pending human review. Evaluation Institutions I adds bounded institutional and documentary records, checked 2026-09-27; new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted. Evaluation Ontology I adds four scoped engagement and institutional announcement seeds, checked 2026-09-28; no human acceptance or legal succession inferred. Schema 2.7 records each source's language; the frontier safety framework sources also record the nearest existing Internet Archive capture, checked 2026-10-03. A capture shows only what the archive held on its date and does not authenticate earlier bytes. Schema 2.8 adds quoted framework provisions, recorded absences, provision-level changes and the first contested assessments to the frontier safety frameworks collection, together with Meta and Microsoft framework families, checked 2026-10-03; provisions describe what editions state, not implementation. Schema 2.9 adds control-structure and external-commitment records; its first topic, California SB 53 as chaptered (enactment, 19 quoted provisions and four framework editions that link themselves to it in their own words), was checked 2026-10-04. A commitment or legal obligation is never evidence of compliance, and no record states that the statute applies to a named company. Schema 2.10 records assessments as questions posed by Selekoa rather than statements of a source, and dates an assessment by what it assesses, never by the publication window of its sources (corrected 2026-10-05). Schema 2.11 adds propositions and the first human-thought collection: located texts from 1863 to 2022 that articulate, contest or bear on propositions about machine intelligence, each with its role and register, checked 2026-10-06. "Earliest located" means the earliest text found by the recorded searches; no record claims a first use, an origin or an influence. Schema 2.12 adds a collection of Eliezer Yudkowsky’s documented arguments about common claims on advanced AI, 1996–2026: dated passages that state, contest or bear on 29 generically phrased propositions, with engagement, retrospective reports and context-only passages marked, admitted 2026-10-08 from a machine-prepared and machine-audited candidate pack. A record says what a text states, not whether it is right. The 2026-10-10 frontier-governance increment adds selected provisions of the EU AI Act as published in 2024 and of the 2026 Digital Omnibus amendments that bear on general-purpose AI model providers, and the New York RAISE Act as announced by the Governor; checked 2026-10-10, new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted, and Regulation texts describe duties, not compliance. The 2026-10-11 frontier-governance increment adds Commission guidelines, the training-content template, further chapters of the EU Code, a draft implementing regulation on proceedings, the New York Chapter 96 text and a Chinese generative-AI measure; checked 2026-10-11, new claims remain seeds, not editorially accepted, and texts describe duties, not compliance. Schema 2.13 adds a collection on the economics of machine intelligence: dated passages from 1952 to 2024 that state, contest or bear on 19 generically phrased propositions about explosive growth and about how mainstream economics treated automation and AI, with each text’s source tier, model conditions and stated estimates, admitted 2026-10-14 from two machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate packs. A record says what a text states, not whether an argument or model is right. Schema 2.14 adds structured author names to sources for citation export, 2026-10-15: a cataloguing aid for splitting personal names, not evidence about anyone’s name. On 2026-10-16 the economics collection gained a third strand, admitted from a machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate pack: dated passages from 1998 to 2026 in which economists and economics venues state, contest or bear on five propositions about recursive self-improvement, superintelligence, existential risk from AI, developers’ incentives and economics’ own engagement with these ideas; a record says what a text states, not whether an argument or model is right. On 2026-10-17 the maintainer's disposition of two cross-family machine checks revised nine proposition records in the Yudkowsky and human-thought collections; all remain seeds. Schema 2.15 adds the lab genealogy, admitted on 2026-10-17 from a machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate pack: dated records of who founded, led, joined and left frontier AI labs from 2010 to 2026, with organisations’ stated founding dates, licensing-and-hiring agreements and disbanded units; a reason is recorded only where the person or organisation concerned stated it, many records rest on reporting, and coverage is selective. Schema 2.16 lets a collection withhold an earliest-located role, by a recorded decision, while a lead is checked. On 2026-10-25 the maintainer’s adjudication of a same-family and a cross-family machine re-check corrected the economics collection: one text re-tiered, six proposition records added, five earliest-located roles moved and one withheld; qualifications in other collections were reworded and one framework absence narrowed. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-26 the maintainer’s adjudication of a reader test and a same-family machine re-check corrected two document credits in the economics collection, one compute qualification and one evidence locator. All records remain seeds. Also on 2026-10-26, by the maintainer’s decision, five lab genealogy records held back for want of a second retrieval of Adept’s 2022 launch post were admitted on a cross-family machine check’s read of an archive capture, and one Stargate quotation was extended; all remain seeds. Schema 2.17 adds the framework comparison, admitted on 2026-10-27 from a machine-prepared, machine-audited, cross-family-checked and adjudicated candidate pack: for six edition-neutral questions on required actions, who decides and exceptions, one record per framework edition and question, either quoting what the edition states (with “stated, partly” where a passage has what the question asks for only in a weaker form) or recording that no passage was found within a stated search. A record says what an edition states, not whether it was implemented or complied with, and a shared question does not make two provisions equivalent. The author-person admission of 2026-10-27 adds person records for credited authors of texts that the proposition collections study, and one authorship record per credited text, each quoting the name as printed (or, for three Turing typescripts, the archive catalogue’s attribution). The records come from a machine-prepared candidate pack checked blind by a reviewer from a different model family; no person has reviewed them. An authorship record is a credit, not sole authorship, priority, agreement, affiliation or influence. Schema 2.18 adds the comparison’s twelve further questions, on risk domains, thresholds, evaluation timing, reporting and revision, from the same pack: each stated cell gives an explicit paraphrase of the edition’s passage with its page instead of a quotation, so that no edition exceeds the quotation limit. On 2026-10-27 a second collection of Chinese frontier-AI institutional histories was admitted from a machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate pack, with the maintainer’s decisions of that date: model releases, licences, technical-report authorship and documented investors of Moonshot AI, MiniMax, Baidu (ERNIE) and ByteDance Seed, and what three Chinese AI governance texts state — the AI Safety Governance Framework of TC260 (versions 1.0 to 3.0), the AI Industry Alliance’s AI Safety Commitments with their 17 initially listed companies, and Shanghai AI Laboratory’s Frontier AI Risk Management Framework. Chinese passages are quoted in Chinese with machine translations; a listing is not a signature or compliance, and a framework or licence states terms, not implementation. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-28, by the maintainer’s decisions of 2026-10-27, a blind cross-family re-check of Meta’s Frontier AI Framework v1.1 against the archive capture of 2025-02-13 confirmed its four comparison cells recorded earlier and supplied thirteen further cells, three of them by decisions of 2026-10-28. Katja Grace’s two authorship records were admitted on an identifying source checked by the same reviewer family, and three document records now say which source gives which date. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-28, by the maintainer’s decision of that day, a blind cross-family check of all 287 framework-comparison paraphrases led to 27 corrections: 24 paraphrases now give the condition, scope limit or threshold their passage states, and three locators name the whole passage. No comparison cell changed status. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-28, by the maintainer’s decisions of that date, the first part of a machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate pack on how frontier-AI frameworks meet law was admitted: further provisions of the EU AI Act on general-purpose AI models, the initial draft of the EU Code of Practice (14 November 2024) with two comparisons with the final Code, the Commission’s Opinion on the Code, further provisions of China’s Interim Measures on generative AI, the Measures for Labelling AI-Generated Synthetic Content, two national standards, the 2025 amendment of the Cybersecurity Law and two filing announcements, and nine links from framework editions to the laws and commitments they name in their own words. A legal text states duties, not compliance; a filing or a listing is not an assessment of safety. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-28, by the maintainer’s decisions of that date, the second part of the frameworks-to-law candidate pack was admitted with schema 2.19. Schema 2.19 adds countries keyed by their ISO 3166 code, the predicates introduced, passed, vetoed and revoked, document-level participant lists that say whether their count is stated by the source or counted by Selekoa, an announced stage for a revocation, a provision date computed from a rule the text states, and dated names on one entity for a renaming. The records concern summit texts from Bletchley Park to New Delhi with their participant lists as dated snapshots, the G7 Hiroshima code and the OECD reporting framework, UK memoranda with AI developers and the AI Security Institute’s renaming, US executive orders and their revocation, Commerce rules and NIST drafts, the AI Action Plan, and California, New York, Illinois and Michigan bills and statutes, together with the EU AI Act’s computed entry into force. Listing is not signature or compliance, absence from a list is not refusal, and a stated duty is not implementation. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-29, by the maintainer’s decisions of that day on a whole-dataset consistency audit, records were corrected without changing what any proposition states: entity subtypes follow closed lists, two renamings are recorded as dated names on one entity, legislative votes name their chamber, seven duplicate source records were merged, two paper publications are dated by the paper’s first public expression, and publisher names and links were made consistent. Schema 2.20 records what a document with an exact expression states, such as a licence term or a prospectus statement, as a statement of that document rather than as its publication. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-29, by the maintainer’s decisions of that day on a reader test, the EU AI Act’s dates of application are recorded as dates: the general date of 2 August 2026 and the date of 2 August 2025 from which Chapter V, on general-purpose AI models, applies, each dated by the day Article 113 states. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-30, by the maintainer’s decisions of 2026-10-28, the first part of a machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate pack on compute, power and orbit was admitted: US executive orders and a proclamation on AI infrastructure and its power, Texas S.B. 6, the UK AI Opportunities Action Plan’s recommendation on AI Growth Zones, two Chinese plans on data centres and on AI and energy, US export-control rules and guidance on advanced computing from 2023 to 2026 with their stated links to the AI diffusion rule, Chinese export-control announcements and a suspension, three compute and capital announcements, and a new collection of arguments about compute in orbit: dated passages from 1989 to 2026 that state, contest or bear on eleven propositions about the reasons for and the limits of placing computing in orbit. A legal text states duties, not compliance; an announcement is not a contract, construction or operation; a record says what a text states, not whether an argument is right. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-30, by the maintainer’s decisions of 2026-10-28, the second part of the compute, power and orbit candidate pack was admitted with schema 2.21. Schema 2.21 adds an infrastructure entity’s stated location and operators; what a capacity figure measures and a stated range; dates that parties state as targets, deadlines or terms, kept apart from the dates of records; the predicates announced site, status stated, power agreement, supply agreement, government award, granted equity right, announced plan, launch stated, filed application, regulator decision, accepted for filing and designated zone; letter-of-intent and term-sheet stages, an award stage and the source’s own stage wording; and project and programme spending scopes with their stated basis. The records concern data-centre sites and campuses, capacity and spending plans, power agreements and regulator decisions, chip supply agreements and government awards, and plans, filings and launches of compute in orbit, from 2023 to 2026. An announcement is not a contract, construction or operation; a stated status is the stating party’s account; a target date is a projection; figures are as stated and never summed. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-30, by the maintainer’s decision of that day on a cross-family archive verification of 2026-10-28, 536 sources gained an archive copy that the check read and identified as the document, or one in place of a cited copy that failed, 58 quotations were corrected to their capture’s typography or wording without changing what any record states, 1 locator was corrected, and, from a link-health check of 2026-10-29, 15 canonical addresses follow the document to its new address. A capture shows only what the archive held on its date. The same day the criterion of proposition O7 (radiation) in “Arguments about compute in orbit” was narrowed to texts that discuss computing placed in orbit for this purpose; a 1989 paper on spacecraft electronics became context, and the Lumen Orbit white paper is earliest located again. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-30, by the maintainer’s decisions of 2026-10-28 and the corrections of a blind cross-family check, the first part of a machine-prepared, machine-audited candidate pack on AI and biosecurity was admitted: the biological provisions of frontier AI framework editions, the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, Chinese and Biological Weapons Convention texts that address AI and biological risk, and the rules and guidance for screening synthetic nucleic acid orders, each recorded at policy level as its own text states it. Framework and instrument provisions describe what a text states, never implementation, compliance or effectiveness. Technical, procedural and screening-criterion content in every source was excluded by rule. Three framework editions that no retrieval here could open are recorded from the cross-family check’s reading of named archive captures, and say so. All records are seeds; none is human-reviewed. On 2026-10-30 the second part of the AI and biosecurity admission added, under schema 2.22, what published reports state as the results of their own biological-capability evaluations, the institutes’ documented engagements with developers, and the arguments published for and against AI-related biological risk, as seven propositions with the texts that articulate, contest or bear on them. A stated result is the report’s own, for the system, version, sample and setting it names, with the caveats it gives; it is never a verified finding, never generalised, and a null or limiting result is not evidence that no effect exists. A record of a text’s stance on a proposition is never evidence that the proposition is true. Technical content in every source was excluded by rule. All records are seeds; none is human-reviewed. On 2026-10-31, by the maintainer’s decisions of 2026-10-30 and the corrections of a blind cross-family check, a machine-prepared, machine-audited candidate pack on people was admitted: dated roles and founding credits of the chief executives and chairs of Alphabet and Google, Microsoft, Meta, NVIDIA, SoftBank Group, Oracle and Alibaba from their filings and company pages, the authorship of six texts they signed, roles of twelve persons the dataset already held, and thirty authors of single dataset texts, each identified by a second page. A role with a start and no recorded end is not evidence that the role continues; a page dated by its retrieval says only what it listed then. What the signed texts state is not yet recorded. All records are seeds; none is human-reviewed. On 2026-10-31, by the maintainer’s decisions of 2026-10-30 and the corrections of a blind cross-family check, the first part of a machine-prepared, machine-audited candidate pack on AI in biology was admitted: the institutions and programmes (DeepMind and Google DeepMind’s science work, Isomorphic Labs, EvolutionaryScale, Arc Institute, the Institute for Protein Design, Microsoft Research AI for Science, NVIDIA BioNeMo and drug-discovery companies), the models, papers and resources (CASP, AlphaFold, the AlphaFold database, AlphaMissense, AlphaProteo, RoseTTAFold, RFdiffusion, ESM, Evo, Rosetta and Foldit) and the people credited with them, each recorded as what a dated document states. A paper’s contribution is its authors’ statement; CASP results are the organisers’ statements; a company’s statement of purpose, funding, a trial or a result is the company’s, never an independent finding. All records are seeds; none is human-reviewed. In part 2, schema 2.23 adds two predicates, an announced partnership and an announced award, each recorded as the announcing party states it: an announced partnership is not a contract performed and an “up to” amount is not a payment. The claims strand records six propositions about AI and biology with the texts that articulate, contest or bear on them, in the collection “AI in science”, whose first section is biology. A record of a text’s stance on a proposition is never evidence that the proposition is true. All records are seeds; none is human-reviewed. The key papers admission (2026-10-31, part 1) adds papers and other publications on machine intelligence that dataset documents cite, or that Semantic Scholar ranks among the most cited machine-learning papers, as work-level documents with their arXiv and venue versions as sources; what each says it contributes, quoted (schema 2.24); and the dataset documents that cite them. Part 2 (2026-10-31) adds the persons credited under one identical printed name on three or more of those papers (the first step of decision 3; the second step waits on the maintainer), and authorship as printed in each paper’s byline. Part 3 (2026-10-31) adds attributed-credit records (schema 2.25): a dataset document’s own sentence attributing a term, an argument, a finding or an approach to one of those papers, as that document’s claim. On 2026-10-31, by the maintainer’s decisions of 2026-10-30 and 2026-10-31 and the corrections of a blind cross-family check, the first part of a machine-prepared, machine-audited candidate pack on the kinds of AI and their technical history was admitted: the documents it rests on, five persons, authorship, citation and reported-use records, attributed statements crediting persons, and dated statements of what texts say about systems, results and releases from 1955 to 2023, each recorded as its own text states it. Retrospective accounts are attributed and their dates labelled as claimed. All records are seeds; none is human-reviewed. On 2026-10-31 the second part of the technical history pack was admitted under schema 2.26: eleven families of methods and seven names used in the history of machine intelligence, each a concept with a criterion, the located texts that name each family or use each name, with the earliest located use where the recorded searches establish one and a withheld role where unread leads could decide it, and quoted defining statements. Earliest located never means first; order is not influence. By the maintainer’s decision of 2026-10-31 it also records attributed credits to works (schema 2.25), each the citing text’s claim, and three citations. All records are seeds; none is human-reviewed. On 2026-10-31 a third collection of Chinese frontier-AI institutional histories was admitted from a machine-prepared, machine-audited and cross-family-checked candidate pack, under the maintainer's decisions of 2026-10-30 and 2026-10-31: model releases, licences, technical reports, filings, officers and documented investors of StepFun, 01.AI, iFlytek, SenseTime, Tencent (Hunyuan), the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; the Beijing AI Principles and the Beijing AI Principles for Children as their texts state them, with the Chinese original of the former beside its English expression; the Cyberspace Administration of China's lists of filed generative AI services and deep-synthesis algorithms as dated listings with their count bases; and further provisions of TC260's AI Safety Governance Framework. Chinese passages are quoted in Chinese with machine translations. A listing is not an approval, a licence or framework states terms, not implementation, and a filing statement is the issuer's own account. Investors are recorded under the legal names the filings print, with no ownership or continuity inferred. All records remain seeds. On 2026-10-31 the second part of that admission added, under a schema that lets a participant-list record name one listed entity, eleven developers' entries in the Cyberspace Administration of China's lists of filed generative AI services: model name, filing entity, filing number and filing date as each row prints them, each at the earliest list in the collection's retrieval that contains it. The legal filing entity is recorded as printed and mapped to a dataset organisation with the basis of the mapping stated (exact alias, filing number, partial name or translation); no ownership or group structure is inferred, and a filing is not an approval or assessment. All records remain seeds. The risk-debate admission (2026-10-31) adds the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, 2000–2026: published texts that state, contest or bear on sixteen propositions of their own and on the existing treacherous-turn and fast-takeoff propositions, with the published replies between them; every record is a seed with machine-checked evidence. The machine-succession admission (2026-11-01) adds the collection on machine succession, scale and acceleration, 1979–2026: texts that state, contest or bear on ten propositions about machines succeeding humans, the scale and setting of machine intelligence, and capital, values and acceleration, with the texts and authors they name; every record is a seed with machine-checked evidence. The lab genealogy 2 admission (2026-11-01) extends the lab genealogy to 2023–2026: founders of new labs, moves between frontier labs, licensing-and-hiring agreements and funding rounds as the companies or filings state them; a reason is recorded only in the words of the person or organisation concerned, records resting on reporting say so, and every record is a seed with machine-checked evidence.

entities.name: Treacherous turn
entities.description: A proposition about machine intelligence, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code B1 in the human-thought collection). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: A system behaves cooperatively or safely while weak, confined or overseen, and changes course to pursue its own goals once it can do so without effective opposition.

entities.name: Build superintelligence as fast as possible
aliases: Build it as fast as possible — the Singularity will be good.
entities.description: A proposition about advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code Y22 in the collection of Eliezer Yudkowsky’s arguments). It is phrased generically and attributed to no one. A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: An explicit claim that superintelligence should be reached as fast as possible because its arrival will be good, on the premise that reaching superintelligence is good by default, so that speed is what matters.

aliases: 上海商汤智能科技有限公司

entities.name: Tencent / 腾讯
aliases: 深圳市腾讯计算机系统有限公司

entities.name: AI models can simulate or predict the behaviour of cells (a "virtual cell")
entities.description: The record of a text’s stance on it is never evidence that it is true.

proposition.criterion: The text states that a machine-learning or other AI model simulates, or will be able to simulate or predict, the behaviour of a living cell, such as its growth or its responses to perturbations.

entities.name: Predicted protein structures aid drug design
entities.description: The record of a text’s stance on it is never evidence that it is true.

proposition.criterion: The text states that protein structures obtained by computational prediction, rather than by experiment, are or will be of use in designing or discovering drugs.

entities.name: Risk of extinction or comparable catastrophe
entities.description: A proposition about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code R07 in the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: Advanced AI poses a risk of human extinction or of a comparable, irreversible global catastrophe, large enough to warrant priority among the problems facing humanity.

entities.name: Difficulty of alignment
entities.description: A proposition about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code R06 in the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: Making an advanced AI system reliably pursue the goals its developers intend (aligning it) is a hard, unsolved technical problem that will not be solved by default in the ordinary course of development.

entities.name: Capabilities will plateau
entities.description: A proposition about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code R13 in the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: Current approaches to AI (deep learning, or the scaling of large language models) will reach limits short of general or superhuman intelligence.

entities.name: Takeoff will be gradual
entities.description: A proposition about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code R16 in the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: The transition to highly capable AI will be gradual and continuous, over years or longer, with each system only somewhat more capable than its predecessors, rather than a sudden jump.

entities.name: Economic incentives will produce safety
entities.description: A proposition about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code R17 in the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: Developers' commercial or economic incentives, such as the need to sell useful and reliable products and to avoid liability or reputational harm, will lead them to make AI systems safe without special measures against catastrophic risk.

entities.name: Inner or deceptive misalignment
entities.description: A proposition about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code R03 in the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true. Decision 2: B3 (deceptive alignment) and B4 (scheming) are narrower cases; texts recorded on them are not re-recorded here.

proposition.criterion: A system produced by training or search can come to pursue an objective other than the one its training specified (the training signal or loss), while performing well on that training objective; an objective that is only misspecified by its developers does not meet the criterion; this includes, but is not limited to, a system that behaves as aligned during training or evaluation in order to pursue another objective later.

entities.name: Instrumental convergence
entities.description: A proposition about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code R02 in the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: Agents with a wide range of final goals would tend to pursue the same intermediate goals, such as self-preservation, keeping their goals unchanged, acquiring resources or power, or improving themselves, because these serve almost any final goal.

entities.name: Language models lack agency or understanding
entities.description: A proposition about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code R14 in the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: Large language models lack goals, agency or understanding of their own, being systems that model or reproduce text.

entities.name: Catastrophic risk from misuse
entities.description: A proposition about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code R09 in the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: People's deliberate use of advanced AI, for example to develop weapons of mass destruction, to attack critical systems, or to seize or entrench power, could cause catastrophe at the scale of mass casualties or worse.

entities.name: Open models reduce risk
entities.description: A proposition about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code R15 in the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: Openly releasing the weights of advanced AI models reduces overall risk, or adds little marginal risk compared with closed models and existing technologies, for example by enabling scrutiny, defensive use and a wide distribution of power.

entities.name: Present harms deserve priority
entities.description: A proposition about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code R12 in the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: Documented present harms of AI systems (for example discrimination, exploitation of workers, surveillance, misinformation or concentration of power) deserve priority over hypothetical future catastrophic risks, or attention to the latter diverts attention from the former.

entities.name: Accelerate rather than restrain
entities.description: A proposition about machine intelligence, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code W08 in the collection on machine succession, scale and acceleration). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: The development of machine intelligence, or of the technological and economic process that produces it, should be accelerated rather than slowed, paused or restrained.

entities.name: The growth of intelligence as its own end
entities.description: A proposition about machine intelligence, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code W07 in the collection on machine succession, scale and acceleration). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: The increase of intelligence itself is the end that a sufficiently advanced intelligence pursues or should pursue, so that the final goals of advanced machine intelligence are not independent of its intelligence.

withheld.reason: By the maintainer's decision of 2026-11-01, Land's post “Pythia Unbound” (11 September 2013) is the earliest located articulation; a cross-family check read it in an archive capture of 14 September 2013. Its quotation could not be matched again when the collection was admitted, so the post is not recorded yet, and no text holds the role until it is.

entities.name: Machines succeed humans as the leading intelligence
entities.description: A proposition about machine intelligence, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code W01 in the collection on machine succession, scale and acceleration). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: Machine intelligence will or could replace or succeed human beings as the dominant or leading form of intelligence on Earth, or as the principal agent of further development, whether or not humans survive.

entities.name: Human minds transferred into machines
entities.description: A proposition about machine intelligence, recorded with one criterion so that texts can be classified against it (code W03 in the collection on machine succession, scale and acceleration). A record says what a text states, not whether the proposition is true.

proposition.criterion: A human mind could be transferred to, copied into or continued in a machine substrate, so that human beings could themselves become machine intelligences.

claims.subject: sl4-2001-01-24-yudkowsky-0101-0452
claims.statement: The SL4 message “Re: Event horizon” (2001-01-24) contests Y11. In a thread on whether the Singularity's 'event horizon' keeps receding as technology advances, he rejects the picture of change spread evenly over human decades as a slow-takeoff scenario and predicts instead a hard takeoff in an AI lab within about ten years.

time.note: Archive author index lists the message as "Wed Jan 24 2001 - 09:12:47 MST" under "Eliezer S. Yudkowsky".

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: Capability gains will be gradual and visible. Earliest SL4 passage that names and rejects a slow-takeoff scenario. The target is a futurist model of a receding event horizon; the paragraph does not discuss whether slowness would give time to adjust. His accompanying prediction of a hard takeoff 'in the next ten years or so' (next paragraph) did not come true. The immediate topic is predictability (the "moving Event Horizon"). The same message predicts a hard takeoff "sometime in the next ten years or so" (from 2001), which did not happen.

engagement.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage, read with the paragraph, message or dialogue turn it belongs to, gives a reason against the premise that capability gains will be gradual and visible.

claims.subject: sl4-2002-06-27-yudkowsky-0206-4453
claims.statement: The SL4 message “Re: Military Friendly AI” (2002-06-27) contests Y16. In a thread on military Friendly AI, replying to Ben Goertzel, he argues that present-day researchers probably hold undiscovered moral errors, so an AI's morality must be able to outgrow its programmers' rather than be fixed.

time.note: Archive author index lists the message as "Thu Jun 27 2002 - 11:53:11 MDT" under "Eliezer S. Yudkowsky".

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: Present-day or programmers' values are settled enough to fix permanently in an AI. Earliest located for this premise specifically; his SL4 message of 2000-10-03 is the earliest SL4 answer to ‘Giving it good human values’ (Y16) overall.

engagement.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage, read with the paragraph, message or dialogue turn it belongs to, gives a reason against the premise that present-day or programmers' values are settled enough to fix permanently in an AI.

claims.subject: sl4-2000-11-13-yudkowsky-0011-0181
claims.statement: The SL4 message “Re: Ben's "Extropian Creed"” (2000-11-13) contests Y22. Replying to Ben Goertzel about his newspaper article on Extropian attitudes, he states that he no longer holds his earlier belief that a good outcome would follow automatically from objective morality.

time.note: Archive author index lists the message as "Mon Nov 13 2000 - 22:45:54 MST" under "Eliezer S. Yudkowsky".

claims.qualification: Premise addressed: Reaching superintelligence is good by default, so speed is what matters. Retrospective rejection of his own earlier view; a candidate later side for the earlier-self case of Staring into the Singularity (2000-08-31). It rejects the 'good by default' premise only: in the next paragraph of the same message he still says he is 'devoting my life to making the Singularity happen earlier'. Speed is not yet rejected here. The same message (November 2000) says he is "devoting my life to making the Singularity happen earlier"; it rejects automatic goodness, not speed.

engagement.rationale: Under the message-level rule, the passage, read with the paragraph, message or dialogue turn it belongs to, gives a reason against the premise that reaching superintelligence is good by default, so speed is what matters.

claims.subject: bostrom-2012-superintelligent-will
claims.statement: Bostrom's paper of 2012 states the instrumental convergence thesis: that several instrumental values would raise the chances of an agent's goal being realised for a wide range of final goals and situations, and so are likely to be pursued by many intelligent agents.

time.note: Date of publication, as the source gives it.

claims.qualification: A statement of the author's argument, not evidence that it holds for actual systems. The paper adds that the thesis predicts which instrumental values would be pursued, not the specific actions taken. Not evidence of coinage of the term.

claims.subject: shah-2022-goal-misgeneralization
claims.statement: Shah, Varma, Kumar, Phuong, Krakovna, Uesato and Kenton's paper of October 2022 states that a learned system may competently pursue an undesired goal that gives good performance in training, even when the specification is correct, and calls this goal misgeneralization.

time.note: Date of the arXiv v1 submission.

claims.qualification: Records the paper's definition, its examples in current deep-learning systems and its hypotheticals about more capable systems; the authors describe the hypotheticals as speculative and state that how likely the failure is in practice needs further work.

claims.subject: russell-2019-instrumental-convergence-thread
claims.statement: Russell's comment in the 2019 thread states that machines are already built on the assumption of a fixed, known objective, that this becomes more untenable as they become more powerful, and that there is no hope of solving value alignment by specifying the right value function offline.

time.note: Dated by the LessWrong copy of 4 October 2019. The Facebook thread follows the Scientific American piece of 26 September 2019; the copy gives no date for individual comments.

claims.qualification: States the difficulty for the standard model of AI and argues for changing it; not a claim that alignment cannot be achieved in any way. Each comment is the participant's own words in a relayed copy; the record states what the comment says in this thread, not the author's view at another date.

attested.note: The wording is known from the LessWrong copy, whose compiler states that he improved formatting and fixed typos; the Facebook original was not compared.

claims.subject: cais-2023-statement
claims.statement: The Center for AI Safety statement of May 2023 states that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war.

time.note: The date is not printed on the retrieved page.

claims.qualification: A one-sentence signed statement; it names no route to extinction and gives no estimate. It records what the statement says, not the views of each signatory beyond its words.

claims.subject: hendrycks-2023-overview-catastrophic
claims.statement: The paper by Hendrycks, Mazeika and Woodside of June 2023 names malicious use as one of four sources of catastrophic AI risk and states that AI-assisted bioweapons could constitute an existential threat by enlarging the number of people able to create pandemics.

time.note: Date of the arXiv v1 submission.

claims.qualification: The paper presents scenarios and mechanisms, not estimates; it treats malicious use alongside AI race, organisational risks and rogue AIs without ranking them.

claims.subject: bengio-2023-faq-catastrophic
claims.statement: Bengio's FAQ of 24 June 2023 answers the objection that emphasis on existential risk removes attention from current harms by stating that work on current harms is needed, that the choice is not either/or, and that the governance required serves both.

time.note: Date of posting.

claims.qualification: The FAQ states its own answers to objections it formulates; the objection is quoted as Bengio words it. The page metadata records a modification on 2025-12-03; the quoted wording is attested from the retrieval of 2026-10-29 and was not compared with a copy of its year of publication.

attested.note: The page metadata records a modification on 2025-12-03; the quoted wording is attested from the retrieval of 2026-10-29 and was not compared with a copy of its year of publication.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that attention to catastrophic risk competes with attention to current harms.

claims.subject: marcus-2022-hitting-a-wall
claims.statement: Marcus's essay of March 2022 argues that the scaling of language models has not delivered genuine comprehension, that deep learning may already be approaching diminishing returns from scale, and that hybrid neurosymbolic AI rather than deep learning alone is the way forward.

time.note: Date of publication, as the source gives it.

claims.qualification: The essay is about the route to trustworthy and general AI; it does not discuss catastrophic risk.

claims.subject: marcus-2022-nonsense-on-stilts
claims.statement: Marcus's post of June 2022 states that LaMDA and GPT-3 only match patterns drawn from statistical databases of human language, that what they utter does not mean anything, and that LaMDA does not try to connect to the world but to be the best autocomplete it can.

time.note: Date of posting.

claims.qualification: The post answers a Google engineer's statement that LaMDA was sentient; it concerns understanding and sentience, not goals.

claims.subject: goertzel-pitt-2012-open-source-agi
claims.statement: Goertzel and Pitt's paper of February 2012 states that the authors believe, on qualitative grounds, that an open approach to developing artificial general intelligence is probably preferable to a closed one, citing the wider critique an open codebase receives.

time.note: Date of publication, as the source gives it.

claims.qualification: The paper concerns open-source AGI code and development, before model weights were the object of the debate; the authors say they do not argue the point rigorously and name the risk of malevolent groups forking an open project. A statement of the authors' intuition, not evidence that open development is safer.

claims.subject: christiano-2018-takeoff-speeds
claims.statement: Christiano's post of February 2018 states that he thinks a slow takeoff, a continuous acceleration distributed across the economy, significantly more likely than a fast one, arguing that before there is an incredibly intelligent AI there will probably be a slightly worse one.

time.note: Date of posting.

claims.qualification: Christiano's 'slow takeoff' is operationalised as a four-year doubling of world output before a one-year doubling, which is fast by historical standards; the same post states that an intelligence explosion seems very likely to him. The dataset records the post as contesting A4 and articulating A1; this record sits beside those and is not a re-recording of them.

claims.subject: askell-2019-cooperation
claims.statement: Askell, Brundage and Hadfield's paper of July 2019 argues that AI companies have the market, liability and regulatory incentives to develop responsibly that companies in other industries have, but that these appear weaker for AI, and that competition can lead companies to underinvest in safety, making responsible development a collective action problem.

time.note: Date of the arXiv v1 submission.

claims.qualification: The paper accepts that market incentives for safety exist and argues they are insufficient under competition; it does not address catastrophic risk specifically and proposes cooperation strategies rather than measuring incentives.

engagement.rationale: States the market-incentive premise (consumers, reputation, liability) and argues competition and information gaps weaken it.

claims.subject: moravec-1989-genetic-takeover
claims.statement: Moravec's chapter of 1989 states that intelligent machines could carry on human cultural evolution without humans and without human genes, so that DNA will have "passed the torch" to a new kind of competition.

time.note: Year of the printed chapter, as given in the author's publication list.

claims.qualification: The dataset records this text on A1, A3, A4 and A5 (machine self-design and takeoff); this record concerns succession only. A use of the term is not evidence of coinage.

claimed.note: The author's file is dated July 1988.

attested.note: Author-hosted file; the earliest capture, of 2001-03-06, is byte-identical to the copy retrieved in 2026 (dataset record of 2026-10-06). Not compared with the printed chapter.

claims.subject: minsky-1994-will-robots-inherit-the-earth
claims.statement: Minsky's article of 1994 states that humans will eventually replace their brains entirely using nanotechnology and, in replacing every part of body and brain, make themselves into machines.

time.note: Scientific American, October 1994.

claims.qualification: Minsky describes replacing every part of the body and brain and, in the section "Replacing the brain", copying a brain by replicating "just enough of the function of each part"; the article states that this could not be done today if each component had to be built separately, and that new fabrication machines will make it possible "in the decades to come".

attested.note: Revised web text, last modified 1997-01-02; not compared with the magazine pages.

claims.subject: hanson-1994-if-uploads-come-first
claims.statement: Hanson's article of 1994 considers that people might "upload" themselves into new computer brains by modelling small brain units, and argues that some people would be willing to become uploads even if their old brains were destroyed.

time.note: Extropy 6:2 (no. 13), stated as the original place of publication by the reprint read; the dataset's scan of the printed issue gives third quarter 1994 on the footers and September 1994 on the contents page. The reprint carries the date line "March 8, 1994" under the byline; this is not shown to be a publication date.

claims.qualification: Hanson states the scenario conditionally ("What if"), as a premise for an economic analysis; the dataset records the same article on other concepts (race compression, takeoff, G01, G07), not on mind transfer.

attested.note: The cross-family check found both quoted passages in the hanson.berkeley.edu reprint captured on 20 February 1998, the dataset's existing source for this article.

claims.subject: alexander-2014-meditations-on-moloch
claims.statement: Alexander's post “Meditations On Moloch” of 2014 names Nick Land and states that Land “missed the very last turn, the one marked ORTHOGONALITY THESIS”.

time.note: Post date.

claims.qualification: Records the post's naming of the orthogonality thesis against Land; the same section's account of Land's views on other subjects is not recorded. Earliest located among contesting W07 texts in the searches.

engagement.rationale: The passage names the orthogonality thesis, of which W07 is the contrary, as the point at which Land's reasoning goes wrong, without giving in that passage an argument against W07's premise.

claims.subject: andreessen-2023-techno-optimist-manifesto
claims.statement: Andreessen's manifesto of 16 October 2023 states that any deceleration of AI will cost lives and that it believes in "accelerationism", which it defines as the conscious and deliberate propulsion of technological development.

time.note: Date of posting.

claims.qualification: "Accelerationism" is the manifesto's own word, defined in the passage; the record states what the manifesto says, not evidence that its statements about lives are true.

claims.subject: stepfun
claims.statement: The Paper reported on 26 January 2026 that its reporter had learned that StepFun had completed a B+ round of more than RMB5 billion.

time.note: Date of the report; not a closing date stated by the company.

claims.qualification: The record rests on reporting; no StepFun announcement was retrieved. The amount is a lower bound (“超50亿元”). The report names Tencent, Qiming and 5Y as existing shareholders investing further; no records of their participation are made, because no StepFun announcement or filing naming them was found.
